This page follows `main` at 9d25dc1, and it differs from the copy in HotLoop 4.17.0, the latest release. Parts of it may be newer than what you have installed. The [release notes](/releases/) say what moved.

Added in 4.14.0. `internal/reports` runs operator-defined reports on a schedule:
it queries the historian, renders the result as CSV and HTML, stores it on a
volume, and optionally emails it. It is the counterpart of Ignition's Reporting
module for the part of that module a plant most often uses, a table of numbers
delivered on time. Off by default (`HOTLOOP_REPORTS_ENABLED`).

## What it is, and what it is not

- **API only.** There is no screen for it in this version. Reports are defined,
  run, listed, and downloaded through `/api/reports`. A UI is a separate piece of
  work.
- **CSV and HTML only.** No PDF. Producing a good PDF in pure Go, with no
  external binary (the runtime image has none, on purpose), means choosing a PDF
  library and a layout engine, and that is a decision of its own. The HTML file
  is self-contained and prints cleanly from any browser, which covers "I need a
  PDF" for now.
- **Tables of aggregates, not free-form layouts.** A report is a list of tags,
  a window, a bucket size, and a set of aggregations. It is not a page designer.
- **One Gateway instance.** The scheduler assumes it is the only thing running
  reports against this database. Two replicas would each fire every report.
  This chart runs one replica, and the reports volume is `ReadWriteOnce`.
- **Not an alarm feature.** Alarm email is `internal/notify`. Reports share its
  SMTP relay settings and nothing else.

## A report definition

Definitions are operator-edited data, stored in the database like devices, tags,
alarm definitions, and fleet members, and managed through the API. Example:

```json
{
  "id": "line1-daily",
  "name": "Line 1 daily summary",
  "enabled": true,
  "tags": [
    {"deviceId": "press-01", "tagName": "Zone1_Temp"},
    {"deviceId": "press-01", "tagName": "Pressure"}
  ],
  "window": {"count": 1, "unit": "days", "end": "local_midnight"},
  "bucket": "hour",
  "aggregations": ["min", "max", "avg", "count"],
  "schedule": {"kind": "daily", "at": "03:00"},
  "format": "both",
  "recipients": ["ops@example.com"],
  "retain": 30
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, dot, dash, or underscore, starting with a letter or digit. It names the report's directory on the volume, so it is validated the way every other id in this app is. |
| `name` | Shown in the HTML title and the email subject. No control characters. |
| `enabled` | Whether the scheduler runs it. A disabled report can still be run by hand. |
| `tags` | 1 to 50 device and tag pairs. Each must exist when the definition is saved, and must not be a string tag. |
| `window` | The span of history each run covers. See below. |
| `bucket` | `window` (one row per tag), `hour`, or `day`. Defaults to `window`. |
| `aggregations` | One or more of `min`, `max`, `avg`, `first`, `last`, or `count`, each at most once. |
| `schedule` | See below. |
| `format` | `csv`, `html`, or `both`. Defaults to `csv`. |
| `recipients` | Optional. Plain addresses only (`ops@example.com`, not `Ops <ops@example.com>`). At most 20. |
| `retain` | How many runs to keep. 1 to 1000. Defaults to 30. |

`PUT` replaces the whole definition. A client can read a report, change one
field, and send it back as it is: the read-only fields the server adds
(`nextRunAt`, `lastRun`, `lastRunAt`, `createdAt`, and `updatedAt`) are accepted
and ignored.

A definition that would produce more than 1000 buckets is refused when it is
saved (hourly buckets over more than about 41 days, for example).

## Windows

A window is relative to when the run happens.

| You want | `count` | `unit` | `end` |
|---|---|---|---|
| The previous 24 hours | 24 | `hours` | `run_time` |
| The previous calendar day | 1 | `days` | `local_midnight` |
| The previous 7 whole days | 7 | `days` | `local_midnight` |
| A rolling week | 7 | `days` | `run_time` |

- `end` is the moment the run starts, or, for `local_midnight`, the most recent
  local midnight at or before it. A run at 03:00 ending at local midnight covers
  whole calendar days.
- **Hours are elapsed time. Days are calendar days** in the plant timezone. A
  one-day window that ends at local midnight is the whole of one local day, which
  is 23 hours long on the day the clocks go forward and 25 on the day they go
  back. "The previous 24 hours" is always exactly 24 hours.
- **A window is half-open**: it includes its start and excludes its end. A
  reading stamped exactly at midnight belongs to the day that starts there. Two
  consecutive daily reports never both count a reading and never both miss it.
- A manual run and a catch-up run compute the window as of the moment they run.

## Buckets

- `window`: one row per tag over the whole window.
- `hour`: one row per tag per local clock hour. A window that does not start on
  the hour begins with a shorter partial bucket, and one that does not end on
  the hour ends with one. Hours stay on the hour across a clock change and in
  zones whose offset is not a whole number of hours.
- `day`: one row per tag per local calendar day.

Every tag has a row for every bucket, including buckets with nothing in them.
The report never omits the hour a sensor was silent, because a report that
quietly left the row out would look the same as one for a sensor that had
nothing to say. Each row states the exact span it covers (`period_start` and
`period_end`, with their UTC offsets), so a 23-hour day shows as one.

## Aggregations and the quality rule

The aggregations are `min`, `max`, `avg`, `first` (the earliest reading in the
period by timestamp), `last` (the latest), and `count`.

Reports follow the quality rule, the same one
the trend chart follows, so a report and a trend over the same hour agree. A
reading with no numeric value (a string reading) is left out too. There is no
switch for it: an average that quietly mixes in readings the historian itself
marked as untrustworthy is worse than a report that says how many it did not
use.

Every row therefore carries an `excluded` column: how many readings in that
period were left out. `count` is how many were used. The run record and the
email carry the totals.

**Nothing is fabricated.** A tag with no usable reading in a period has no
minimum, and the report says so: the cells are empty in the CSV and read
`no data` in the HTML. They are never zero. Zero is a reading (a valve closed,
a flow of nothing) and is aggregated like any other value. `count` is the one
column that is a number when there is no data, because zero is a true count of
nothing.

## Schedules and time

A schedule is one of:

```json
{"kind": "interval", "every": "6h"}
{"kind": "daily",    "at": "03:00"}
{"kind": "weekly",   "weekday": "monday", "at": "06:30"}
```

- An **interval** is elapsed time (at least one minute) and ignores the wall
  clock.
- **Daily and weekly** times are wall-clock times in the plant timezone, which is
  `HOTLOOP_TIMEZONE` (the chart's `global.timezone`). It must be a real zone
  name such as `America/Chicago`. An unusable name is a refused start, reports
  on or off, not a quiet fall back to UTC, because a report meant for 03:00
  local that fires at 03:00 UTC is a bug nobody sees until the numbers are wrong.

### Daylight saving

The next run is computed by building a wall-clock time in the plant's location
with `time.Date`. It is never computed by adding 24 hours to the previous run,
which fires an hour early or an hour late from one clock change to the next.
Two wall-clock times are awkward on a change day, and the rule for each is fixed
in code rather than left to `time.Date`, whose behavior for both is documented
as unspecified:

- **A time that does not exist** (02:30 on the spring-forward day, when the clock
  jumps from 02:00 to 03:00) fires at the first instant after the gap, 03:00. It
  runs late by at most the size of the gap and does not skip the day.
- **A time that happens twice** (01:30 on the fall-back day) fires once, at its
  first occurrence.

### last_run_at, the next run, and catch-up

`last_run_at` is when the scheduler last **started** the report, whether that run
then succeeded or failed. A manual run does not move it, so running a report by
hand at 02:00 does not cancel tonight's 03:00 run.

The next run is the first scheduled time after the latest of the definition's
creation, its last edit, and its `last_run_at`. Measuring from the last edit
means moving a report from 03:00 to 09:00 at 10:00 waits for tomorrow instead of
firing at once for a time that had already passed.

**Catch-up.** If the next run after `last_run_at` is already in the past when
the Gateway starts, the Gateway was not there to make it, and the report runs
**once**, immediately, labeled `catchup`. It is not run once per missed time: a
daily report that missed three days runs once, on the day the Gateway comes
back, with the window that means as of now. The missed days are not backfilled.
After that the report is back on its schedule.

`last_run_at` is written **before** the run starts, so a Gateway that dies
mid-run does not repeat the run on restart on top of an email that may already
have gone out. The interrupted run is recorded as failed instead. A failed
scheduled run is not retried; the next scheduled time runs normally, and
`POST /api/reports/{id}/run` is there when someone wants it again.

## Output

Each run writes its files under `HOTLOOP_REPORTS_DIR` (`/data/reports`, a PVC in
the chart):

```
/data/reports/<report id>/<UTC timestamp>-<run id>.csv
/data/reports/<report id>/<UTC timestamp>-<run id>.html
```

- **File names are built only from a validated id, a UTC timestamp, and the run's
  integer id.** Path traversal is closed off by construction: the report id must
  satisfy the same identifier rule as everywhere else, and a file name read back
  from a run record is matched against the exact pattern above before it is
  opened. The `{run}` in a download URL is parsed as an integer and used only to
  look up the run record together with the report id. The file that is opened is
  the one that record names. Nothing from the URL becomes part of a path.
- Files are created with `O_EXCL` and mode `0640`, and directories with `0750`.
  A file that already exists is an error, never overwritten. The output holds
  plant data and tag names, so the mode is a floor, not a substitute for
  protecting the volume.
- **Retention.** After every run the newest `retain` runs that stored files are
  kept, and older ones are deleted with their files. Failed runs, which have no
  files, are kept separately (the newest `retain` of those), so a run of
  failures cannot push the last good report out. Any file in the report's
  directory that matches the naming pattern but is not referenced by a
  remaining run record (the partial file of a run that died) is removed as well.
  A file that does not match the pattern, such as one an operator put there, is
  left alone.

### CSV

RFC 4180, from `encoding/csv`, with CRLF line endings. The columns are
`device_id`, `tag_name`, `unit`, `period_start`, `period_end`, one column per
aggregation in the order the definition lists them, and `excluded`. Timestamps
are RFC 3339 in the plant timezone with their offset. Numbers are written at
full precision.

**Spreadsheet formula injection.** A tag name or a unit is text somebody typed,
and a spreadsheet reads a cell that begins with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` as a
formula. Any text cell that begins with one of those (or with a tab or carriage
return, or a space followed by one) is prefixed with an apostrophe, which
spreadsheets treat as "this is text" and do not display. The numeric columns are
written from numbers, so a negative reading is left alone and still reads as a
number.

The file has no byte order mark. Excel opens a UTF-8 CSV without one as if it
were a legacy code page, so a tag name with non-ASCII characters may need to be
imported as UTF-8.

### HTML

One self-contained file, built with `html/template`, so tag names and values are
escaped for where they land: a tag called `<script>` is written as text. The
stylesheet is inline and there is no script, font, image, or link to anywhere,
because deployments can be air-gapped. It also carries a
`Content-Security-Policy` meta tag that forbids loading anything, and the API
serves it with a policy that adds `sandbox`, as an attachment.

## Delivery by email

If a report has `recipients`, each run emails the files as attachments, through
the SMTP relay configured under `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_*` (host, port, username,
password, from, TLS). Only the relay is shared with the alarm channel: whether
that channel is enabled, and who alarms go to, have no effect on reports, so a
deployment can email reports without paging anyone. The chart writes the relay's
variables for reports alone when the alarm channel is off.

It is the same SMTP code as the alarm channel, not a second copy. `internal/notify`
gained one general function, `SendMessage`, that sends a message with attachments
to a list of recipients. The alarm channel now sends through it as well. The
connection handling is unchanged (port 465 now speaks TLS from the first byte,
see [NOTIFY.md](/iot/notifications/#implicit-tls-port-465)): STARTTLS whenever the relay offers it, `AUTH`
when credentials are set, and a hard failure before `AUTH` when
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS` is set and the relay does not offer STARTTLS. For an
ASCII alarm the message is the same bytes as before, apart from the `Date`
header, and a test pins that. A non-ASCII alarm subject is now sent as an
RFC 2047 encoded word instead of raw UTF-8.

The message is `multipart/mixed`: a quoted-printable text part, then each file
base64-encoded. **Header injection is refused, not cleaned.** Recipients, the
sender, the subject, and the attachment file names are validated: a value with a
CR, LF, or other control character in it, a recipient in display-name form or
holding a list, or a file name with a quote or a path in it makes the message
fail before anything is sent to the relay. The alarm channel's own subject is the
one exception, because a page must go out whatever an alarm is called: it
flattens control characters to spaces first.

- **No relay configured.** A report with recipients still runs and stores its
  files, and the run is recorded as `failed`, with `emailStatus` `failed` and an
  error that says the relay is not configured. It does not succeed silently.
- **Too big.** `HOTLOOP_REPORTS_MAX_EMAIL_BYTES` (10 MiB) caps the attachment
  data in one email. A report over it is stored and downloadable, and its run
  records why it was not emailed.
- A run made by hand can skip the email with `?deliver=false`.

## Run records and the audit trail

Every run is recorded in `report_runs` from the moment it starts: when it
started and finished, the trigger (`schedule`, `catchup`, or `manual`), who
asked, the window, the outcome and error text, the number of tags, rows,
readings aggregated, and readings excluded, the files stored, the email outcome
and its recipients, and notes (for example, that a tag has since been deleted and
is being reported from its recorded history). Success and failure are also
written through `rt.Event`, the same audit trail alarms and fleet actions use,
with the report id as the subject.

A run cut short by shutdown, by its time limit (`HOTLOOP_REPORTS_RUN_TIMEOUT`),
or by the report being deleted is recorded as failed with that reason. A run left
`running` by a process that died is marked failed when the Gateway next starts.
Only one run of a report is in flight at a time; a second request while one is
running is a `409`.

## API

| Route | Permission | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/reports` | `reports.read` | Every definition, each with its `nextRunAt` and most recent run |
| `POST /api/reports` | `reports.write` | Create. `409` if the id exists |
| `GET /api/reports/{id}` | `reports.read` | One definition |
| `PUT /api/reports/{id}` | `reports.write` | Replace. The id cannot change |
| `DELETE /api/reports/{id}` | `reports.write` | Delete, with its runs and files. A run in flight is cancelled first |
| `POST /api/reports/{id}/run` | `reports.run` | Run now and wait. `?deliver=false` skips the email |
| `GET /api/reports/{id}/runs` | `reports.read` | Run records, newest first (`?limit=`, up to 500) |
| `GET /api/reports/{id}/runs/{run}/download?format=csv\|html` | `reports.read` | Stream one stored file as an attachment |

`POST .../run` returns the run record with `200` whether the run worked or not.
The status says whether the request was carried out, and the record's own
`status` says whether the report was. A run that fails is a result, and it is
recorded either way. The run is not tied to the client's connection: hanging up
does not abort a report that may already have started an email.

With the feature off, the list answers `{"reports": [], "configured": false}` and
every other route answers with an error naming `HOTLOOP_REPORTS_ENABLED`.

### Who may do what

| Role | `reports.read` | `reports.run` | `reports.write` |
|---|---|---|---|
| viewer | yes | no | no |
| operator | yes | yes | no |
| admin | yes | yes | yes |

- **Read** is for viewers because a stored report is aggregates of history a
  viewer can already read through `values.read`, so reading or downloading one
  grants nothing new.
- **Run** is for operators because running a report only ever delivers to the
  recipients an admin already chose, and it can be run without delivering.
- **Write is admin-only.** A definition names the addresses its output is emailed
  to, so being able to define one is being able to send plant data to an
  arbitrary address on a schedule. That is closer in kind to `notify.test` and
  `fleet.config` (also admin-only, also "do something to the outside world") than
  to a read. This is a judgment call, and could be revisited if a real workflow
  needs operators to build reports.
- An operator can still cause an email to go to a report's recipients by running
  it, and repeatedly. There is a one-run-at-a-time guard and `?deliver=false`, but
  no rate limit.
- A user with an explicit permission list holds exactly what it names; the
  `reports.*` wildcard covers all three.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_REPORTS_ENABLED` | `false` | The feature is off, including the scheduler, until this is set |
| `HOTLOOP_REPORTS_DIR` | `/data/reports` | Where each run's files are written. Meant to be a PVC (`reports.persistence` in the chart) |
| `HOTLOOP_REPORTS_RUN_TIMEOUT` | `5m` | Bounds one run: query, render, write, and email |
| `HOTLOOP_REPORTS_MAX_EMAIL_BYTES` | `10485760` | The most attachment data in one email |
| `HOTLOOP_TIMEZONE` | `UTC` | The plant timezone. Must be a real zone name, or HotLoop won't start |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_HOST`, `_PORT`, `_USERNAME`, `_PASSWORD`, `_FROM`, `_TLS`, `_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY` | | The relay reports email through. See [NOTIFY.md](/iot/notifications/) |

The chart's `reports` block has `enabled`, `runTimeout`, `maxEmailBytes`, and
`persistence` (size, storage class, access mode). `notify.smtp` supplies the
relay. Reports are not started in `--mcp-stdio` mode, which is an agent spawning
the binary as a helper, and a second scheduler beside the real Gateway would run
every due report twice.

## Backups

Report definitions and run records are user data and are part of the database
backup (`internal/backup`). The output files are not: they are on the reports
volume, and restoring a backup into a new deployment brings back the records but
not the files, so downloading an old run there answers that the file is no
longer on disk. Copy the reports volume if the files matter.

Adding these two tables to the backup list is the kind of change that is easy to
forget, so the backup package now has guards for it. One test lists every table
in the schema and fails if any is in neither `backup.Tables` nor an explicit
exclusion list with a reason. Another checks that `Tables` is in foreign-key
order, reading the foreign keys from the database. The round-trip test seeds a
report definition and a run and checks the restored values and the sequence.

## What has and has not been verified

This repository distinguishes **tested** from **verified**, and this feature is
tested. Nothing in it has been verified against a specific mail provider or a
specific spreadsheet application.

**Tested**, against real infrastructure and not mocks:

- The historian aggregation, against a real `timescale/timescaledb:2.29.1-pg16`,
  in both storage modes: the TimescaleDB hypertable and the native-partitioning
  fallback. The same plain SQL (a join, `width_bucket` against a boundary array,
  and ordinary aggregates) runs in both. Every cell of a stored CSV is compared
  with values worked out independently in the test from the seeded readings,
  including hours with no data, an hour with only bad readings, bad and uncertain
  readings among good ones, negative values, a zero, a reading exactly on an hour
  boundary, and readings on either side of the window.
- Delivery, against two real SMTP servers ([axllent/mailpit](https://github.com/axllent/mailpit),
  run with Podman, never Docker): a bare one, and one that requires STARTTLS and a
  login. The message is read back through Mailpit's HTTP API and the test checks
  the recipients, the subject, the body, and that the bytes of each attachment
  equal the file the run stored. A wrong password is recorded as a failed run.
- The scheduler firing on its own (a moving clock, no call to the run function),
  the catch-up run and that it is only one, and the daylight-saving cases at the
  level of the schedule and of the scheduler: 03:00 stays 03:00 across the
  spring-forward and fall-back days in `America/Chicago`, the previous calendar
  day is 23 and 25 hours on those days, and a schedule that added 24 hours would
  fail these tests.
- The lifecycle under the race detector: repeated start and stop, and a run held
  open in the database while it is edited, deleted, stopped, and timed out.
- The HTTP surface, through the real router: every route against a role or
  explicit permission list that has and lacks each permission, path-traversal
  attempts in the report id, the run number, and the format, and downloads.
- Several of the tests above were proved by mutation, by breaking the code and
  watching the test fail. The pull request lists them.

**Not verified**:

- Any specific mail provider or gateway. STARTTLS and implicit TLS on port 465
  both work, the same as the alarm channel (see
  [NOTIFY.md](/iot/notifications/#implicit-tls-port-465)); neither has been tried against a
  commercial provider.
- Any specific spreadsheet application. The formula-injection defense is the
  standard apostrophe prefix, checked by parsing the CSV, not by opening it in
  Excel, LibreOffice, or Google Sheets.
- A browser rendering of the HTML file. It is checked for escaping, for being
  self-contained, and for what it says, not for how it looks.
- Zones whose clock changes are not a whole hour (Lord Howe Island, 30 minutes)
  go through the same code, and a half-hour offset is tested for hour buckets, but
  such a change itself is not.
- Very large windows or many tags. The limits (50 tags, 1000 buckets, 20
  recipients) are enforced and tested, and query time at the top of them on a
  large historian has not been measured.
- Clocks. The scheduler trusts the Gateway's clock, and the database's for a
  definition's created and edited times.
